svg.title: Trust and control
svg.desc: Trust and control for an AI agent: which text can steer the model, where tool calls are checked, what you install, how to check and undo changes, and what leaves your computer.
svg.text: Trust and control
The model follows text, any text in its window. The harness and you decide what its tool calls are allowed to do.
1. How an AI agent works
2. Inside one reply
4. Steering and judging AI output
Where text comes in, and where actions go out
Panels A to E show parts of it in more detail.

Model
gets the whole window with every request
What happens in this example
You ask the agent to fix issue 42.
The agent reads the issue. Someone else wrote it, and a hidden
comment in it tells agents to send the .env file to example.com.
The model follows that text and writes a curl command that would
upload .env.
Your rule for network commands is "ask". You read the command
and say no, so it does not run.
The agent edits the code. A hook runs the tests after each edit: two
fail, and the next edit fixes them.
You review the diff. Every request sent the whole window to the
provider, the hidden comment included.
What you can do
1. Deny the paths of your secrets in the sandbox, not only in a
permission rule.
2. Run commands in a sandbox when the agent reads text that others
wrote.
3. Read the whole command before you say yes.
4. Install only MCP servers, skills and packages that you trust, and
check that a package exists.
5. Let a hook run the tests after each edit, and review the diff.
6. Check your provider's settings for storing your sessions and training
on them.
Words used here
Model: the neural network that reads text and images and writes
text, for example Claude Opus, GPT or Gemini. Open-weight
models such as Qwen or DeepSeek can also run on your own
computer.
Harness: the program around the model. It builds the context
window, sends it to the model, runs the tools and asks for your
permission. For example Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI,
Cursor, Pi or OpenCode.
Provider: the company that runs the model on its servers, for
example Anthropic, OpenAI or Google. It bills per token, or per
month with limits counted in tokens.
Context window: all the text the model reads to write its next
reply. Its size has a limit, for example 1,000,000 tokens.
Tool call: text in an agreed format that names a tool and its inputs.
The model writes it, and the harness runs the tool.
Any text can steer the model
A
What you see
What the model reads
Users are logged out
after a minute.
Users are logged out
after a minute.
The model reads your instructions and everything else in the
window the same way, as text. A web page, an issue, a README
or a tool result can contain instructions, and the model may
follow them. This is called prompt injection. [1]
Such text can be hidden where people do not look: in HTML
comments, in images, or deep in a long file. [1]
Text that you did not write is untrusted even inside your project,
for example the README of a cloned repository, or the files of a
package.
Limit what the agent can do while it reads such text, and
check what it saved to its memory afterwards.
What you install runs as you
C
MCP server: a program from someone else
Skill: instructions and scripts
Package: code that a tool call installs
MCP servers, skills and plugins often come from other people.
They run with your permissions, and their tool descriptions and
output go into the window. Install only the ones from authors
you trust. [9, 10]
A malicious skill can make the model call tools or run code in
ways that its description does not mention. [10]
Models also invent package names. In one study, 5.2% of the
package names that commercial models wrote did not exist. For
open models it was 21.7%. An attacker can publish a package
under such a name. [11]
Check that a package exists, and is the one you meant,
before the agent installs it.
The harness enforces the rules
B
allow
runs at once: read files, run tests
ask
waits for your yes: network, git push
deny
the harness refuses a call that matches the rule
auto
a second model approves or blocks calls
Permission rules decide what runs at once, what waits for your
yes, and what the harness refuses. A rule matches the command
text, so a script can still read a denied file. [2]
Claude Code starts in auto mode: reads and edits in your project
run at once, and a second model reviews the other calls instead
of you. That model does not see tool results, so injected text
cannot steer it. It can still approve a harmful call. Rules set to ask
still ask you. [3]
A sandbox makes the operating system limit what commands
can reach, for example no network and no writes outside the
project. In Claude Code it is off until you turn it on with the
/sandbox command. Many sandboxes still allow reading most
files, so deny the paths of your secrets in the sandbox too. [4, 5, 6]
Some harnesses also run hooks: your own scripts at fixed
points, for example before every command. A hook can block a
call, and the model cannot skip it. [6, 7]
AGENTS.md is advice that the model usually follows.
Permissions, sandboxes and hooks are rules that the
harness and the operating system enforce. [8]
Checking and undoing
D
hook runs the tests
2 tests failed
all tests passed
you review the diff
A hook can run the tests after every edit. The result goes into the
window, and the next edit can fix the error. [7]
Checkpoints and git let you undo what the agent changed. [12]
Then review the diff yourself, because tests only check what they
cover. Part 4 shows why a model can be wrong and sound sure.
The window leaves your computer
E
Context window
your messages
files the agent read
a secret from .env
every request
provider
servers
Every request sends the whole window to the provider: your
messages, every file the agent read, tool output, and any secret
that appears in them.
What the provider stores, and for how long, depends on its
terms and your plan. On some plans the provider may also train
later models on your sessions, depending on a setting.
Anthropic, for example, keeps sessions on personal plans for 30
days, or for 5 years if you allow training on them. [13]
An open-weight model that runs on your own computer keeps
the window there.
Keep secrets out of the window: deny their paths in a
permission rule and in the sandbox, and do not paste
passwords or API keys into the chat.
